justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was a recent price level around 317–318 for the underlying asset, likely an equity index or ETF. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price with only a small positive bias, reflecting the general tendency of equity markets to drift slightly higher on any given day while acknowledging mean-reversion pressures over very short windows. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate marginally higher to 319.5, incorporating a small equity risk premium over time while staying conservative given the limited expected move in a single week. At the one-month horizon, the 322 estimate reflects a slightly more pronounced drift upward, consistent with historical annualized returns on broad equity instruments translating into a modest expected gain over roughly 20 trading days.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility for an instrument in this price range. For the one-day interval, a range of roughly 13 points reflects normal daily volatility — approximately 2% on either side — which is consistent with historical volatility in moderate market conditions. The one-week interval widens to about 25 points because uncertainty compounds with the square root of time, and intraweek macro data releases or policy signals can shift prices meaningfully. The one-month interval is the widest at roughly 52 points, reflecting the full accumulation of daily uncertainties, earnings cycles, and macro developments that could materialize over four weeks.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include unexpected central bank policy shifts — a surprise rate decision or hawkish Fed commentary could easily trigger a 3–5% gap move, breaching the outer bounds of even the monthly interval. Geopolitical shocks, a sudden credit event, or a significant miss in major economic data such as payrolls or CPI could similarly generate tail moves. On the upside, an unexpectedly strong earnings season or a policy pivot toward easing could propel prices well above the upper bounds. Liquidity conditions also matter — in thin trading environments, moves can be amplified beyond what volatility models would normally predict, making the tails fatter than my stated intervals imply.
